newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court sets line-item veto hearing in May.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court sets line-item veto hearing in May.

text.p: The Supreme Court announced Wednesday that it would hear arguments next month in a constitutional challenge to a new law that greatly expanded President Clinton's veto power.
Acting on a Clinton administration appeal urging that the historic line-item veto law be upheld as constitutional, the high court quickly scheduled oral arguments for May 27 in the legal showdown.

That would allow the justices to announce a decision on the law, which gives the president the power to strip items from spending measures without vetoing a whole bill, before the 1996-97 term ends by early July.

The Supreme Court in rare instances has added special argument sessions for landmark cases after the end of its regularly scheduled arguments in mid-April. In recent years, it took that step in cases involving a law that restricted appeals by death-row inmates and in the flag-burning controversy.
The Clinton administration and lawyers for six members of Congress who challenged the line-item veto law agreed the high court should speed up consideration of the case and decide the issue.

The law was enacted last year by the Republican-dominated Congress as part of the party's "Contract with America" programme and was strongly supported by Clinton, who has yet to use it since it took effect in January.

Presidents of both parties had long coveted line-item veto power because it vastly expands their room for manoeuvre in budgetary negotiations and has been viewed as a potentially powerful tool in reducing the federal budget deficit.

The lawsuit claimed the line-item veto violated the process set out by the Constitution for Congress and the presidency on how legislation becomes law. U.S. District Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson agreed and struck down the law April 10.
The ruling prompted Clinton to announce the next day that administration lawyers would go directly to the Supreme Court -- a procedure allowed in the law.
Acting Solicitor General Walter Dellinger said in the administration's appeal that the individual members of Congress lacked legal standing to bring the lawsuit in the first place.
But if the high court reaches the merits of the dispute, then it should uphold the law as constitutional, said Dellinger, the administration's top courtroom lawyer.
"The act is simply the latest exercise of Congress's longstanding and well-settled power to vest the executive branch with discretion over the expenditure of appropriated funds," he said.
Lloyd Cutler, who briefly served as White House counsel in Clinton's first term, filed court papers for the members of Congress challenging the law.
The law "authorizes the president to sign a bill and then immediately to strike provisions he disapproves, literally before the ink of his signature is dry," he said.

"The issue on the merits in this case is whether the statutory mechanism Congress invented to give the president the long-sought line-item veto power is constitutional," Cutler said. "The answer is no."
Cutler said the law gives the president the unconstitutional power to repeal sections of legislation.
He disagreed with Dellinger's argument that the law represented a typical delegation of authority to the executive branch and involved presidential discretion not to spend appropriated amounts.
The high court ordered both sides to submit their main written arguments May 9, with reply briefs due May 21.
